title: Birdsong! Prelude and Fugue No.10, Book I
content_blocks: Olivier Messaien’s interest in birdsong helped inspire this pair’s fugue. Like Messaien, I’m an amateur birder, and my love of birdsong has inspired me over my forty-year career as a composer. As a brash 21-year old visiting London, I asked Witold Lutosławski what he had to say to those who assert that tonality is ‘natural’ while atonality is…artificial; he responded (so kindly and considerately) that birds don’t sing tonal music, their songs are atonal (that opened my eyes—and ears!). In this fugue I’ve put into practice some of Messiaen’s birdsong tricks, and along the way have learned just how right Lutosławski was.

The entire fugue subject is direct from the song of the Hermit Thrush; having been a hermit during much of 2020, when I composed the piece, I figured this would be suitable material. Plus the song of the Hermit Thrush is truly gorgeous. The main trick from Messaien? Slowing down the birdsong by a factor of about 4, and transposing it down a couple of octaves. Having subjected it to those transformations I figured further octave transposition would be appropriate. As for Lutosławski, how stunning it was to realize that the Hermit Thrush’s song is full of tritones and minor seconds, along with perfect fifths. (Move over, Webern, the Hermit Thrush uses more “atonal triads” than you did!)

Aside from a two-part canon in the center of the fugue—as if two thrushes on either side of me were singing a beat and just over three octaves apart—there is one joke.  This is a four-voice fugue, but by the time the fourth voice shows up the first voice has already flown away, and the second is about to.  So, really—it’s a three-voice fugue, with a straggler.  By the end of the fugue, that straggler is left alone, singing fragments of its song.  The early bird may get the worm, but the late bird gets the last word!

The prelude sets the stage for the fugue by slowly moving up along the scale of the mode. The mode is built out of a three-octave pattern without any notes (such as C or F-sharp) repeated. The three-octave pattern is then repeated up three octaves and a semitone, before returning to the starting pitch-class six octaves higher than the lowest note. Because of this structure there are only specific spots where a note in the upper three octaves will be the same as a note in the lower three octaves; it is these spots where the upward-moving lines overlap and start again on a lower note. There are never more than three overlapping lines at once; despite the slow pace, because of the huge amount of real estate they cover—a total of six octaves!—there are spots where this piece can be very challenging to play. Steve Beck handles it with ease, though: it amazes me how he can move his hand two feet away and have it land on precisely the right half-inch-wide key without so much as a glance—as you can see in the Prelude and the Fugue.
My character name for this prelude and fugue was ‘The Hermit’, which I guess is still appropriate.  This particular hermit does a lot of birdwatching!
The entire fugue subject is the song of the Hermit Thrush.
